description: Test your knowledge of PA RN1 | Renal Pathology I: Glomerular Disease & Renal Failure.

cards.text: Name the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier and identify which provides the charge barrier to exclude negatively charged proteins.
cards.answer: 1) Fenestrated endothelium (size barrier), 2) Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) — charge barrier with heparan sulphate proteoglycans, 3) Podocytes with slit diaphragm (size barrier). The GBM repels anionic albumin due to its heparan sulphate content.

tip.tip: Remember 'E-B-P': Endothelium, Basement membrane (charge), Podocytes — GBM is the charge barrier because it's negatively charged.

cards.text: What is foot process effacement and what pathological condition is it the ultrastructural hallmark of?
cards.answer: Foot process effacement is flattening of the interdigitating foot processes of podocytes seen on electron microscopy. It is the ultrastructural hallmark of nephrotic-range proteinuria.

tip.tip: Effaced feet can't filter — think of flattened podocytes losing selective permeability and allowing protein leakage.

cards.text: Describe the three functional properties of mesangial cells and identify which is particularly important in diabetic nephropathy.
cards.answer: Mesangial cells are 1) Contractile (regulate capillary surface area), 2) Phagocytic (clear immune complexes), 3) Proliferative. Mesangial expansion is an early marker of diabetic nephropathy.

tip.tip: 'CaPP' — Contractile, Phagocytic, Proliferative. In diabetes, think 'expansion' of these cells as a key early sign.

cards.text: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs what percentage of filtered sodium and is vulnerable to which two major types of injury?
cards.answer: The PCT reabsorbs ~67% of filtered Na⁺, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate. It is most vulnerable to ischaemia and toxins due to its high metabolic demand (abundant mitochondria and brush border).

tip.tip: 67% = more than two-thirds. High metabolic demand = high vulnerability. Remember PCT as the injury 'hotspot.'

cards.text: What are the three components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and what stimulates renin secretion?
cards.answer: The JGA comprises 1) JG cells (afferent arteriole wall), 2) Macula densa (DCT patch), 3) Lacis cells (bridging cells). JG cells secrete renin in response to decreased perfusion pressure or low tubular NaCl concentration detected by the macula densa.

tip.tip: 'Low pressure, low salt, renin recall' — JG cells release renin when blood pressure drops or NaCl is depleted.

cards.text: Which tubular segment is the target of loop diuretics and why is it unique among tubular segments?
cards.answer: The thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle is the primary target of loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide). The TAL is unique because it is impermeable to water but actively transports NaCl, creating the medullary concentration gradient.

tip.tip: TAL = 'The Avid Loop' — actively pumps salt but keeps water out. Loop diuretics block this salt pump.

cards.text: What is the structural composition of the glomerular basement membrane and its two key barrier functions?
cards.answer: The GBM is composed of type IV collagen, laminin, and heparan sulphate proteoglycans. Its two key functions are: 1) Size barrier (excludes RBCs and large proteins), 2) Charge barrier (negative heparan sulphate repels anionic albumin).

tip.tip: 'CLH' — Collagen, Laminin, Heparan sulphate. GBM blocks big things (size) and negative things (charge).

cards.text: In rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, what proliferative structure forms from Bowman capsule and which layer is responsible?
cards.answer: The parietal epithelium of Bowman capsule proliferates to form crescents in rapidly progressive GN. These cellular crescents fill Bowman space and indicate aggressive disease with poor prognosis if untreated.

tip.tip: Crescents = crescent-shaped proliferations. The parietal (outer) layer proliferates, not the visceral (podocyte) layer.
